record.paper_title: Infrared tip-tilt sensing: on-sky experience, lessons learned and unsolved problems
record.original_question: How should next-generation infrared tip-tilt sensors be designed to keep the sensor wavefront quality high when non-common-path aberrations between the science detector and the tip-tilt sensor, and anisoplanatic residuals across the field, can degrade the point-spread function at the sensor? In particular, when should the tip-tilt sensor be placed inside the science instrument, when is a deformable mirror needed in the tip-tilt-sensor path, and how can deformable mirrors be characterized or operated in cryogenic sensor environments?

evidence.quote: IR TTSs are sensitive to residual wavefront aberrations. For a diﬀraction-limited core, the sensitivity of the sensor is inversely proportional to the Strehl ratio. We have to optimize the performance not only on the science target, but on the NIR TTS as well.

However, any non-common path aberration between the science detector and the TTS will lead to wavefront errors at the TTS. To mitigate this, instruments under design include the TTS inside the science instrument. In addition, it may be necessary to to incorporate a DM in the path of the TTS, especially if we need to correct for anisoplanatism. Work is under way to chacterize the behavior of existing DMs in a cryogenic environment.
This section addresses issues which must be considered in the design of the next generation of IR TTSs.

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Consider an adaptive-optics system whose science detector operates at near-infrared wavelengths and is fed by a tip-tilt sensor (TTS) also operating in the infrared. The TTS measures the centroid of a guide-star point-spread function (PSF) and provides a two-axis tilt correction to a fast steering mirror. The sensitivity of such a TTS, when the guide-star PSF has a diffraction-limited core, is inversely proportional to the Strehl ratio at the sensor focal plane; hence the residual wavefront quality at the TTS directly determines noise propagation into the tip-tilt loop. Two distinct error sources degrade the TTS PSF:
 (i) Non-common-path aberrations (NCPA): static or quasi-static wavefront errors arising in optical elements that lie in the TTS arm but not in the science arm (or vice versa), and which therefore are not sensed by the high-order wavefront sensor that flattens the science path.
 (ii) Anisoplanatic residuals: residual wavefront errors at the TTS due to the angular separation between the guide star used by the TTS and the high-order wavefront-sensor reference, sampling different turbulent column volumes.

Develop a design framework for next-generation infrared TTSs that answers the following sub-problems:
 (a) Formulate a quantitative criterion, in terms of NCPA amplitude, anisoplanatic angle, atmospheric C_n^2 profile, guide-star magnitude, and required tip-tilt residual variance, that determines when the TTS must be placed inside the cryogenic science instrument (sharing optics with the science detector up to a beam-splitter as far downstream as possible) versus in a separate warm bench.
 (b) Derive conditions under which an additional deformable mirror (DM) in the TTS optical path is necessary to restore a diffraction-limited PSF at the TTS, distinguishing the regimes where only low-order NCPA correction is needed from regimes where dynamic anisoplanatic correction is required.
 (c) Specify a measurement and operational protocol for characterizing the influence-function, hysteresis, stroke, response time, and surface-figure stability of a deformable mirror operated in a cryogenic environment (T ≲ 100 K), and analyze how degradation of these parameters at low temperature propagates into the TTS error budget and final on-sky Strehl ratio.
artifact.status_search_result: The question concerns an open instrumentation design problem for next-generation infrared tip-tilt sensors on extremely large telescopes. Public literature on instruments such as MICADO/MAORY, HARMONI, GMTIFS, and IRIS shows that NCPA mitigation strategies, in-instrument TTS placement, and cryogenic DM characterization are active areas of ongoing R&D rather than settled topics, with experimental DM cryogenic tests still being reported. No comprehensive solution exists.

status_evidence.title: Cryogenic testing of deformable mirrors for astronomical adaptive optics
status_evidence.snippet: Reports ongoing experimental characterization of MEMS/voice-coil DMs at cryogenic temperatures, indicating the problem is unresolved.
status_evidence.claim: Cryogenic DM behavior is still under active experimental investigation.

status_evidence.title: HARMONI / MICADO adaptive optics design overviews
status_evidence.snippet: ELT first-light instruments include IR TTSs inside the cryogenic science instrument and discuss NCPA and anisoplanatism as outstanding design drivers.
status_evidence.claim: In-instrument IR TTS placement is being adopted but design trade-offs are still open.
